Aquatic plants: Plants that grow in water are called aquatic plants.

Floating plants: Plants that float on water are known as floating plants.

Adaptations: They have light and spongy stems so they can easily float on water. Their roots hangs loosely.

Ex: Water Hyacinth and Duckweed

Fixed Plants

Plants have roots fxed to the bottom. They are found in shallow water. Ex: Lotus  and water lily.

They have flat and broad leaves

Their leaves have a waxy coating

Their stems are thin, long and hollow.

They have stomata on the upper surface of leaves which help them to absorb and release gases.

Underwater plants: Plants that grow under the surface of water.

Adaptations: They have thin and narrow leaves. They absorb and release air directly through their surface.

Ex: Tape grass and Pondweed

Some other adaptations:

Insectivorous plants: Plants that feed on insects are called insectivorous plants.

Adaptations:  The Venus flytrap plant has leaves like boxes with hinges. When an insect sits on the leaf and touches the hair, the leaf gets closed, and the insect gets trapped.

Pitcher plant has leaves in the form of pitcher with lid to cover the mouth.When insects sits on the pitcher they get trapped.


Non Green Plants:

They do not have chlorophyll.

They absorb food from dead and decaying plants.

Ex: Indian Pipe and Coralroot.

content.en:
Need for Adaptation

In order to survive in slow changing environment animals need to adapt.

Animals also need to adapt in order to find food, water, air, shelter.

They also need to raise their young ones and protect them from predators.

 

Adaptations in Terrestial Animals


Animals that live on land are called terrestial animals.

• The place where a living organism lives in nature is called its habitat. 
•  Features that help a plant or an animal to survive in its natural surroundings are called adaptations.
• Animals show modifications in their body shape according to the environment and the food that they eat.
• Some of the modification seen in animals to adapt to their environment are

 

1. Snow-covered regions: Temperatures are always extremely cold in the polar regions.
• Animals have a thick coat of fur which helps them keep warm.
• Some animals have a layer of stored fat in their skin which helps to keep the body warm. Penguins have thick fat  layer called blubber which helps them to keep warm.
• E.g. Polar bear, Yak

Some animals like hedgehogs go into winter sleep called Hibernation.

 

 

2. Tropical rainforests: Rainforests have a large cover of tall trees.
• Animals have tails, adhesive pads on their limbs, skin that camouflages with the surroundings, etc.
• Birds have a long beak to eat fruits.
• E.g. Red-eyed frog, monkey, etc.

 

3. Desert environment: The temperatures are always high in the desert environment.
• Water is conserved by secreting thick urine. Camels have thick pad of fat under their feet from sinking into the sand.
• Muscles are adapted to store water. They  stay long without drinking water.
• Slow breathing is observed which reduces the amount of water loss. Summer sleep is the characteristic feature.
• E.g. Camel, desert rat, etc.

title.en: Adaptation through modification of body parts

content.en:
Adaptations according to feeding habits: According to the feeding habits, animals have certain modifications or adaptations that help them to consume food.
1) Herbivores: The animals that consume plants are known as herbivores.
• Animals have teeth that are suitable to chew and grind plants.
• They do not have sharp teeth as they do not need to feed on animals for their food.
• Since they have to travel long distances in search of food, they have long and strong legs.
• E.g. Cow, camel, bullock, etc.

2) Carnivores: Animals that feed on other animals are known as carnivores.
• The teeth of the animal are modified so that they can tear the other animal.
• The canines are long, sharp, and strong that help them to tear the animal's skin and eat the flesh.
• Carnivorous birds have a strong, and sharp beak that helps them to tear the flesh of their prey.
• E.g. Lion, Tiger, Eagle etc.

3) Omnivores: Animals that can consume both plants and animals are known as omnivorous animals.
• The dentition is modified to consume both plants and meat.
• They do not have sharp canines but have broad molars and premolars.
• E.g. Humans, bears, etc.

4) Parasites: The animals that live either on the surface or inside the body of another organism is known as a parasite.
• The organism on which the parasite depends on for its nutrition is known as a host.
• They can cause damage to the host organism and in some cases kill the host organism.
• E.g. Bed bug, mosquito, liver fluke, etc. 

Adaptations for protection: Animals undergo certain modifications or adaptations to protect themselves from their predators. 
• Some of the adaptations are as follows:
a. Small fishes have strong fins and a streamlined body to swim fast in the water and escape their predators.

b. The size of some animals such as elephants, whales, etc. prevents them from being predated.

c. Some animals such as the leaf insect have an appearance that resembles their surroundings and avoids being spotted by the predator. Such an adaptation is known as camouflage.

d. Turtles and snails have shells for protection.

e. Deer have strong legs to run from predators.

f. Porcupine have spines.

content.en:
1. Air occupies space:

Air is matter and all matter occupy space. Air fills up the space around us.

When we put a crumpled tissue paper inside an empty glass and hold the glass inverted over a dish filled with water, the tissue paper remains dry and at the top due to the trapped air occupies space in the glass and does not allow water to enter in.

When we blow a balloon, air fills inside it. This is compressed air to fill a small space. Such compressed air is used to fill tyres, footballs, basketballs, etc.

  1. Air has weight:

An inflated balloon weighs more than an empty one. The air filled inside the balloon causes its weight to increase, making it heavier.

  1. Air exerts pressure:

Air has weight so it exerts pressure. If we keep our hand in lateral position, a lot of pressure is exerted on our hand by the air but we do not feel it. This is because the pressure is being exerted by air in all directions as well as on our hand. As a result, the pressure is balanced out.

  1. Air can carry sound:

Sound from any source like a speaking person, speaker, music system etc. travel through sound waves that enter our ears and strike our eardrum making it audible to us.

  1. Air carries smell:

We are able to smell the scent of flowers when we enter a garden full of flower. This proves that air carries the smell to our nose.

  1. Air produces sound:

Musical instruments like flute, trumpet, bagpipe, shehnai, clarinet, etc. are played by blowing air into it.

content.en:
Air Pollution:

  • Air pollution occurs when unwanted and harmful gases, dust particles, fumes or odour are introduced into the atmosphere in a way that makes it harmful to humans, animals and plants. 

              

Causes of Air Pollution:

  • Air pollution is caused as a result of different human activities.
  • Factories and industries release smoke and other harmful gases.
  • Smoke released from burning of garbage and bursting crackers.
  • Fumes from car exhausts contain dangerous gases. 
  • Heavy metals released by industries.
  • Burning of solid wastes.

Effects of Air Pollution:

  • Air pollution can make people sick.
  • It becomes difficult to breathe and causes diseases such as lung cancer, respiratory and heart diseases.
  • It can trigger an asthmatic attack (a respiratory infection).
  • Some types of air pollution can cause harm to the ozone layer present in the atmosphere. 

Preventive measures

  • Industries should filter out harmful pollutants.
  • Energy efficient boilers should be used.
  • Industries should be away from residential areas.
  • Less polluting fuel such as CNG should be used.
  • Burning of garbage and wood to be avoided.

content.en:
Matter: Anything that has mass and occupies space is called matter.
• The three states of matter are solid, liquid, and gas.
Book, pen, pencil are solids. Water, milk, oil are liquids and oxygen, nitrogen, and water vapours are gases.

            
Change in the state:
• When a substance is subjected to a change in temperature or pressure, the substance can undergo a change in the state of the matter.
• Melting is a process through which a solid can be converted into a liquid state by heating.
• Ice melts and changes into the water on heating.

Other examples: Melting of ice cream and candle wax.

• The process by which liquid changes into a gas is called evaporation.
• Example: Water evaporates and changes into water vapour form.
• Evaporation can be increased by providing heat to the liquid.
• Water can be converted into water vapour by evaporation.

• Rate of evaporation is slow at low temperatures but when we heat a liquid it becomes faster.

• The process by which a gas changes into liquid on cooling is called condensation.
• On cooling, water vapour changes into water.
• Example: Ice cold water in a glass left in open, water droplets are formed on the outer surface of the glass.

Liquid to solid:

• The process by which liquid is converted into a solid on cooling is known as solidification.
• Freezing comes under the category of solidification. On cooling ( freezing), water solidifies into ice.

What happens to the particles present in the matter when they are subjected to heat treatment or cooling?

• Heating and cooling affect the particles which are present in matter irrespective of the state (Solid, liquid, gases) of it.
• When any matter is subjected to heating, the particles present in it starts moving or starts moving faster.
• When they are cooled, the particles present slow down their movement.

content.en:
Solution = Solute + Solvent
• The substance in which the solute gets dissolved is known as the solvent.
• The solute is the substance that gets dissolved in the solvent.
• Water is known as a universal solvent as many substances get dissolved in water.
• A solute and solvent together make up the solution.


• If a substance gets completely dissolved in the solvent, the substance is known as soluble substance. E.g. Salt in water. A few gases such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, are soluble in water.
• If a substance does not completely dissolve in a solvent, the substance is known as an insoluble substance. E.g. Chalk powder in water. Gases that are insoluble in water are hydrogen, nitrogen, and helium.
• When two liquids are mixed completely without forming separate layers is known as miscible liquids. E.g. Alcohol in water.
• When two liquids do not mix completely and form two separate layers is known as immiscible liquids. E.g. Oil in water.
• When two immiscible liquids are mixed, the lighter liquid floats on the top of the heavier ones. So, when oil is dissolved in water, oil is lighter than water, therefore it starts floating in its surface.

Method of separation of soluble substances:
• Evaporation: Soluble substances present in a solution can be separated by the process of evaporation.
Example: Salt dissolved in water can be separated by the process of evaporation.

Methods of separation of insoluble substances:
Insoluble substances can be separated from a liquid by the process of filtration, sedimentation, and decantation.
• Filtration: In this process, the liquid containing insoluble substances are poured onto a filter paper which is placed inside a funnel.
As soon as the liquid is allowed to pass through the filter paper, the insoluble part remains on the filter paper whereas the liquid part moves through it.

• Sedimentation and decantation: In sedimentation, the liquid containing the insoluble substances are allowed to stand without any disturbance for some time.
The heavy and insoluble substances settle down at the bottom of the container. This process is called sedimentation.
• The process in which insoluble impurities settle down is called sedimentation.


• The clear liquid is poured out very gently into another container without disturbing the impurities.
• The process which involves pouring of water gently into another container is called decantation.
• Sedimentation and decantation can be used to separate mud from water.

Objects which give out light are called sources of light.

There are two types of sources of light – Natural and Artificial

Natural Sources of Light:

  • Natural objects that give off light and are not made by man are called natural sources of light.
  • Sun is the main natural source of light on the Earth.
  • Others are the stars and the moon.
  • Moon does not have its own light.It reflects sun’s light that falls on it.
  • Stars gives us very little light as they are very far from us.
  • Animals like glow worms and fireflies also emit light.

Artificial Sources of Light:

Objects which emits light and are made by man for their use are called artificial sources of light

An electric bulb, a tube light, earthen lamp, kerosene lamp and wax candle

  • Luminous Object: Objects which give out light of their own are known as luminous objects. For example; sun, an electric bulb, a candle, and a lamp.
  • Non Luminous Object:Objects which do not have their own light are called non-luminous objects. For example; A chair, cup, toy, book and the moon.

content.en:
1. Light is a form of energy. It always travels in straight line.
2.Light travels in all direction from its source.
3.When light falls on the surface of an opaque object, it bounce back. This is known as reflection of light. When the reflected rays of light reaches our eyes, we are able to see the objects.
4. When light passes from one medium to another, bending of light takes place at the boundary of two media. This is known as refraction of light.
5. Visible light can be split into seven colours – violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, and red (VIBGYOR). This can be seen when light passes through a prism. The formation of rainbow takes place through splitting of light.
6. Light travels very fast.

Materials such as wood, cardboard do not allow any light to pass through them. Such materials are said to be opaque.

Materials like butter paper and coloured glass allow only some light to pass through them. This materials are called translucent.

Materials like clear water, cellophane, glass allow light to pass through them completely.They are said to be transparent.

Measurements:

Measurement is a unit of measuring some object.

⇒Standard Units:

While measuring we need a fixed unit that everyone uses, that is we require a standard unit.

There are three different standard units of measurement:

∙LENGTH

1 Centimetre and metre:

Length is measured in terms of Centimetre or metre.

The standard unit Centimetre, in short, is written as cm.

For measuring longer lengths metre scale or measuring tape is used.

The standard unit Metre, in short, is written as m.

 

Conversion:

One metre equals to hundred centimetres.

1 m=100 cm.

A metre scale is 100 cm long.

mcm845+8501695

∙WEIGHT

To find out which object is weighing more we weigh different objects on a weighing scale.

Mass of an object never varies but weight of an object is changed based on its location.

As we can see that weighing scales are used to measure the weight of the laddoos.

Standard unit:

The standard unit of weight is GRAM and KILOGRAM.

To weigh light objects the standard unit Gram is used and gram is written in short as g 

To weigh heavy objects the standard unit Kilogram is used and a kilogram is written in short as kg.

1 kilogram equals to 1000 grams.

1 kg=1000 g.

The standard weights of 5 kg, 2 kg &1 kg are used to weigh different objects correctly.

We know that,

Rajjo had a bag weighing  5 kg 450 g. She transfers some objects weighing 3 kg 200 g from her bag to her friend's bag. Find the total weight of her bag now.

Weight she transfers from her bag to her friend's bag=3 kg 200 g.

kgg5450-32002250

Ans. Therefore, the total weight of the bag with Rajjo at the end will be 2 kg 250 g.

 

∙Capacity

The amount of liquid in the container is the capacity of the container.

Measuring cylinder is used to measure volume.

Standard unit:

Litre and Millilitre:

To measure the capacity of a small container we use the standard unit Millilitre. In short, it is written as ml.

To measure the capacity of the bigger container we use the standard unit Litre. In short, it is written as l.

Conversion:

1 litre=1000 millilitre

1 l=1000 ml

content.en:
Time:

  • Clocks or watches are used to tell time.
  • Second is the standard unit of time.
  • Time can also be measured in hours, minutes, days, etc.
  • In ancient times, shadows were used to take note of the time.

Clock:

A clock is a device that measures time. With the advent of the clock, measuring time became much easier. 



The clock has three hands:

  • The small hand in a clock is the Hour hand. It moves the slowest.
  • The long hand in a clock is the Minute hand.
  • The hand which shows seconds is the Second hand.

The earth takes 24 hours to complete one rotation around its own axis. 

These 24 hours make a day. 

Daytime and nighttime together form a day of 24 hours. 

Hours are divided into minutes, and minutes are further divided into seconds. 

  • There are 60 minutes in 1 hour. 
  • There are 60 seconds in 1 minute. 

 

Temperature

  • The hotness and coldness of a body is given by temperature.
  • A body having a higher temperature is a hot object and a body having a lower temperature is a cold object. 
  • Temperature is measured by a thermometer.
  • Mercury is filled inside the thermometer.
  • It is the mercury which moves in a clinical thermometer and it should be shaken well before use.


  • Degree Celsius or Fahrenheit is the unit of temperature.
  • The normal body temperature of human beings is about 37-degree celsius.

Push and pull:

i. While pushing an object you hold the object and use your strength to move it forward. The object moves away from you. For example, closing a door.

ii. While pulling an object you hold it and use your strength to move it towards yourself. The object moves closer to you. For example, opening a door.

Force as Push:

Push is defined as the force that is responsible for an object to move from the state of rest away from the source of force.

Examples of push:

  • Pushing the trolley.
  • Pushing of the car when it breaks down.
  • Pushing the table from one place to another.

Force as Pull:

The pull is defined as the force that is responsible for an object to move from the state of rest but in the opposite direction when compared to the push i.e towards the source of force

Examples of pull:

  • Pulling the curtain.
  • Dragging the box.
  • Opening of the door.

Force and its types:

i. Force is a push or pull acting on an object.

ii. Force can move an object, stop a moving object, change the direction of movement of an object, and change the shape of an object. Force can be of many types, such a gravitational force, frictional force, magnetic force, and muscular force.

iii. The force that pulls every object downwards towards the centre of the Earth is called the force of gravity or gravity.

iv. The force that acts whenever any two objects rub together or come in contact is called frictional force or friction.

v. The force with which a magnet attracts certain metals, such as iron and nickel, towards itself is called magnetic force.

vi. The force exerted by the muscles to do work is called the muscular force. Running, walking all are examples of muscular force.

title.en: Friction and how to reduce it?

content.en:
• Friction is the force resisting the relative motion of solid surfaces, fluid layers, and material elements sliding against each other. 
  • Friction can be reduced in many ways.
  • By making the surfaces smooth. The more thesurface is smooth, The lesser is the friction.
  • By use of lubricants. Oil reduces friction.
  • By the use of powder. Ex: Carrom board
  • By the use of grease an wax.
  • By streamlining.

Civics is a study of the rights and duties of citizens that helps us to understand human rights, duties and responsibilities.

Citizen: A person born in a country, enjoys the rights and duties of the country.

Good Citizen: Active participation in community, honest, respects country, aware, responsible, protects neighbourhood and environment.

Participation in Election:

  • Every Indian citizen above the age of 18 years has the right to vote
  • Works as a tool to check the responsibility and accountability of the leaders Protection of Public

Two types of property:

  • Public: The public property is owned by the public, and everyone has a right over it.
  • Private: Owned by an individual, organisations, etc.

Two types of public property

  • First one consists of the building and service that help us to survive such as roads, hospitals, schools, etc
  • Other consists of our Cultural Heritage such as Taj Mahal, forts, etc.

a. Caring for School Property: Damaged property can harm the people and put extra pressure on schools and parents

b. Caring for Monuments: Historical importance as they promote our history through statues, coins, pictures, etc.

Measures taken by the Government

  • PWD works for the maintenance of all the public properties
  • The archaeological department also works for the maintenance

content.en:
• Nicolaus Copernicus was the first person to discover that:
(i) The sun is stationary, and the earth moves around it.
(ii) Earth rotates on its own axis.
• Axis: An imaginary line running from north pole to south pole. It is tilted at an angle of  66 12°..
• Earth has two types of motion:
RotationRevolutionMovement of earth on its own axisMovement of earth around the sunIt takes 1 day (24 hrs) to complete one rotationIt takes 365 14 days to complete one revolutionIt causes day and nightIt causes seasons

Seasons:
• Seasons change due to rotation and revolution of the earth; and the tilting of axis of the earth.
• Northern Summer: Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the sun for six months, it gets more sunlight and heat in the Northern Hemisphere.
• Northern Winter: Northern Hemisphere tilts away from the sun for six months, it gets less heat and sunlight. So it is winter in Northern Hemisphere.
Solstice: It is used to describe the exact moment when the sun reaches its Northernmost point (around 21st June) or the Southernmost point (around 22nd December) from the earth's equator.

Summer solstice Winter solsticeOn 21st June, the direct rays of the sunare falling on Tropic of Cancer.This position of the earth is known as Summer Solstice.On 22nd December, the rays of the sunare falling on Tropic of Capricorn.This position is called Winter solstice. It is summer in Northern HemisphereIt is summer in Southern Hemisphere

Equinoxes:
• When the earth moves around its orbit, it reaches two points during a year, where the tilt of the earth's axis causes it to be straight relative to that of the sun. These days are called equinoxes.
• Spring equinoxes: On 20-21st March, the rays are directly falling on the equator, causing the duration of day and night equal throughout the earth. It is spring in the northern hemisphere, so it is called spring equinoxes.
• Autumnal equinoxes: On 22-23rd September, the rays are directly falling on the equator, causing the duration of day and night equal throughout the earth. It is autumn in the northern hemisphere, so it is called autumnal equinoxes.
• A year: 
- There are 365 days and 6 hours in a year. The time taken by the earth to complete its one revolution around the sun is called one year.
- A leap year consists of 366 days. In a leap year, the February month has 29 days instead of 28 days.
• Rituchakra: In our country, we have summer, rainy, and winter seasons. We divide the year into six seasons, namely, Vasant, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemant, and Shishir. The cycle of these six seasons is called the 'rituchakra.'
• Phases of the moon: 
- The moon revolves around the earth, and the earth revolves around the sun.
- The sun, moon, and the earth are not always in a straight line.
- The moon doesn't have its own light, and we can see the moon only because of the sun's light, which falls on it. 
- We see the whole side of the moon on a full moon night while on a new moon night, we cannot see any side of the moon.
- From new moon to full moon, the moon changes its shape every day.                                                                                                                                                          - From full moon to new moon, it becomes smaller and smaller and after 14 to 15 days it is new moon again and this period is known as Waning.                                    - From new moon to full moon, it again grows bigger and bigger and this period is known as Waxing.                                                                                                          - The different shapes of the moon that we see, are called the phases of the moon.

title.en: The Four Domains of The Earth

content.en:
• Domains of the Earth:
• There are four realms of the Earth, also known as the four spheres of the life that interact with each other, are the Atmosphere, Biosphere, Lithosphere, and Hydrosphere.
• Atmosphere is a blanket of gases surrounding the Earth, which is held in place by the Earth's gravitational pull. The atmosphere extends up to approximately 1600 km above the Earth's surface. The air in the atmosphere consists of majorly Nitrogen (78.1%), oxygen (20.9%), and argon (0.9%). Traces of several other gases like carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, nitrous oxide, hydrogen, helium, neon, ozone, and methane, etc. are also present in the air.

• Importance of atmosphere:
• Life supporting gases such as oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide are present in the atmosphere.
• The atmosphere prevents the harmful ultraviolet rays of the sun from reaching us.
• The atmosphere traps solar radiation and keeps the Earth warm.

• Various layers of the Earth’s atmosphere: 

1. Troposphere
2. Stratosphere
3. Mesosphere
4. Thermosphere
5. Exosphere

• The troposphere is the first layer stretching from ground to 8km-18km above the Earth's surface. This layer is the most important because the air we breathe is present in this layer. All weather changes, such as the formation of clouds, rainfall, etc. as well as human activities, takes place in this layer.

• The stratosphere lies above the troposphere extending up to a height of 50 km. The ozone layer present in this layer protects us from the harmful ultravoilet rays of the sun. Jet aircrafts are allowed to fly in the stratosphere because this layer is very stable.

• Mesosphere lies above the stratosphere, extending up to a height of 50-80km. It is the coldest part of the Earth’s atmosphere.

• The thermosphere stretches from 80-500 km above the surface of the Earth. The temperature is extremely hot in the thermosphere and gets warmer as we go higher. Here the air becomes thinner. At the lower level, this layer contains electrically charged particles. This layer is also known as the ionosphere, as it transmits radiowaves back to the Earth. The space shuttle orbits in this layer.

• The exosphere is the topmost layer or the uppermost limit of the atmosphere. It extends from 500-10000km. It contains light gases like hydrogen and helium. The tempreature is extremely hot in this layer.

• The biosphere is the interlinking zone where land, water, and air come in contact with each other. Life exists only in the biosphere, thus making Earth a unique planet. The biosphere is that part of the Earth where all the living beings exist and where the Lithosphere, Hydrosphere, and Atmosphere co-exist. Earth has countless species of plants and animals living in the biosphere. The biosphere consists of different ecosystems having their own climate, plants, and animals. The physical environment(i.e., the air, water, and land) and the biological environment( all living beings) are both interdependent on each other.

• The lithosphere is the outer solid layer of the Earth, including the Earth's crust and outermost mantle. It is 100km deep from the Earth's surface. The outermost layer that is known as the Earth’s crust varies in thickness. The oceanic crust below the oceans is about 5-10 km. The continental crust is about 35 km under the continents and about 60 km under the mountain ranges. The Lithosphere includes several landforms such as plateaus, plains, mountains, valleys, and ocean floors. 

• Continents are large land masses separated by expanses of water. The seven continents are Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, and Australia.

• Importance of Lithosphere:
• The lithosphere provides the surface on which human beings and animals live, and plants grow. 
• It provides the soil cover and is also a source of minerals.
• It is a source of fossil fuels which fullfills our energy needs.
• Hydrosphere is the water that surrounds all of us.
• It includes all the water on the Earth in any form: Solid form, such as snow and glaciers. Liquid form such as oceans, seas, rivers, lakes, and underground water. Gaseous form such as vapours and moisture in the atmosphere. All life depends on water. 97% of the total water on the Earth's surface is found in oceans and seas.

• Importance of Hydrosphere: 

• Life exists on Earth due to the water cycle. The amount of water vapour in the air affects the weather.
• Water helps in the generation of electricity.
• Water is required for irrigation and everyday needs.
• Marine life in the oceans provides a source of food and livelihood.

• Protection of four realms of Earth:

• Due to the increasing pressure of rapidly growing population and ever increasing demands of humans beings, natural resources are being recklessly exploited.
• Excessive use of insecticides and pesticides are polluting our land and soil quality.
• Pollution caused by various industries and vehicles is polluting the air, water, and land on the Earth.

• Global warming:

• Carbon dioxide traps the heat radiated from the Earth’s surface like a blanket, which results in the increase in the temperature of the Earth's surface. This is called the greenhouse effect. Due to the increase in the level of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, the temperature of the earth increases, which is known as global warming.

• Oceans are very large water bodies separated by continents.

• There are five oceans on the Earth:
• Pacific Ocean
• Atlantic Ocean
• Indian Ocean
• Antarctic Ocean
• Arctic Ocean

• The Pacific Ocean is the largest of all the Oceans and Arctic is the smallest.

content.en:
• Landforms - Landforms are the physical features on the earth's surface that form boundaries between the countries, states, provinces, etc.
• Various types of landforms are Mountains, Plains, Valleys, Plateaus, Hills, etc.

1. Mountain: Mountain is a high area with a steep slope that has an elevation greater than 1,000 ft. Above the sea level. They have different heights and shapes. When many mountains join together, they form a chain, and this chain is called as Mountain range. Mt. Everest is the world's highest mountain, at the height of 29,029 ft. above the sea level.

• Importance of mountains:
a. They form a natural barrier against the hot and cold winds.
b. Mountains are rich in mineral resources and are home to rich flora and fauna.
c. The cooler climate in the mountains attracts the tourists.

2. Plateau: Plateau is a mountain with a flat top having steep slopes. They are also called as tableland because of their shape. The highest plateau is the Plateau of Tibet. The oldest plateau is the Deccan plateau.

• Importance of plateau:
a. Plateaus have rich black soil.
b. Plateaus have waterfalls and have deep canyons. For e.g., Jog falls in Karnataka and Grand Canyon in the USA.
c. The natural scenic beauty of the plateaus attracts the tourists.

3. Plains: Plains are vast stretches of flat grassy areas. The plains are divided into Coastal plains and interior plains. Plains cover 55% of the earth's land surface, and approximately 90% of the earth's population lives on plains.

• Importance of plains:
a. Provide fertile land for cultivation.
b. Plains are thickly populated and provide employment opportunities.

4. Deserts: A desert is a vast land covered with sand. It is found in the north-western part of our country and is called the Thar desert. A desert has scanty rainfall and no rivers. Cactus plant is found in abundance, and camel is an important means of transport in the desert.

• Importance of deserts:
a. We obtain table salt, gypsum, fossil fuels, natural gas and oil, copper, gold, diamond, iron ore, etc. from the dessert.

• Water bodies:
1. River is any natural stream of water that flows in a channel, and finally meets the ocean, or a sea, a lake, or another river. A river has its origin or source in the snow melting region or springs. It flows down the mountain valleys and plains into larger water bodies like lakes, oceans, and seas. It follows its path, called a course, and ends at a mouth.

• During its course, a river goes through three different stages:
a. The upper course:  In this course, the river is in its youthful stage and flows rapidly. It erodes and cuts through the mountains and forms waterfalls, gorges and canyons.
b. The middle course:  In this course, the speed of the river slightly decreases as it flows through gentle slopes. Here, the tributaries join the river, and thus it becomes broad. A tributary is a small stream or a river that joins a big river. As the flow of the river decreases, it starts depositing silt on both sides, thus making the plains fertile. It forms meanders or horse-shoe like loops.
c. The lower course: In the lower course, the flow of the river slows down. It branches out into many smaller streams known as distributaries before it enters the sea. It deposits sediments, thus forming deltas. A very famous delta in India is The Sunderbans formed by the river Ganga in its lower course.

• Importance of rivers:
a. Rivers provide water which we use for various purposes like irrigation, washing, cleaning, etc.
b. Water is also required in industries for various processes.

2. Oceans are huge water bodies separated by continents. There are five oceans on the earth:

i. Pacific Ocean
ii. Atlantic Ocean
iii. Indian Ocean
iv. Southern Ocean 
v. Arctic Ocean

3. Sea is a huge body of saltwater surrounded in whole or in parts by land. 

4. Lakes are fresh or saline water bodies in the natural depressions on the earth's surface. They range in size from a small pond to large areas of hundred square miles.

• Importance of lakes:
a. The water from the lakes can be used for everyday household use, agricultural use, and industrial use.
b. Lake water can be used for hydroelectric power generation.
c. Lakes are tourist spots.
d. Fishing activity can be carried out in lakes.

• A map is a drawing representing the whole area or a part of an area on a flat surface.
• A map represents a small part of the earth’s surface or the entire earth.
• Maps show us various places like the continents, countries, states, districts, cities, or neighbourhoods.

• Merits of maps: 
1. Maps tell us the size and shape of the countries and distance between the places.
2. A map may even show a smaller area with great details such as the exact location of the houses and streets in a city or a neighbourhood.
3. Maps are easy to carry around.

• Limitations of maps: 
1. The earth is round in shape, and a round surface cannot be shown accurately on a flat paper.

• Map scale: Map scale is defined as the ratio of the distance between two places on a map and their actual distance on the ground between those two places.
• The map scale is of two types: 
a. A large scale map which represents a small area in great details.
b. A small scale map represents a large area in less detail.

• Directions: There are four cardinal directions i.e, East, West, North, and South.
• The sub-directions are North-East, North-West, South-East and South-West.

• A compass is an instrument which shows directions. The magnetic needle in the compass always points to the North-South direction. 

• Types of maps: 
1. Physical maps: Maps which shows physical features of the earth like the mountains, plateaus, oceans, rivers, and lakes are called physical maps.
2. Political maps: Political maps show the international borders, location of states, districts, and cities. These maps use different colours to show different countries.
3.Thematic maps: Thematic maps represent only certain features like distribution of minerals, forests, types of weather, etc.

• Signs and symbols: We use symbols to represent the natural or man-made features on the earth, such as buildings, trails, roads, bridges, and rivers.
• A symbol is a dot, line or a drawing that represents something. For example; black dots represent cities, circled stars represent capital cities, and different types of lines represent boundaries, roads, highways and rivers.
• These symbols on a map are called as conventional symbols.

• Colours: Sometimes, colours are used as symbols to share information on a map. Different colours are used to represent different things on the map.

• On a physical map, the colour scheme followed is: 
1) Blue: Water bodies
2) Green: Plain areas
3) Brown: Mountains, Deserts
4) Dark yellow or light brown: Plateaus

• A map usually consists of a key that provides the scale of the map and also explains about the various symbols used in the map.

1) Delhi:
• Capital of India. Also known as the National Capital Territory.
• Delhi- Third largest city in India.
• Haryana and Uttar Pradesh - neighbouring states.
• Delhi city is situated on the banks of the river Yamuna.
• New Delhi was designed and planned by Sir Edwin Lutyens.
• Delhi is the seat of power and centre of political activities in India.
• All the Central Government offices are situated in New Delhi. Also, the President and the Prime Minister reside in Delhi.
• Rashtrapati Bhawan is the residence of the President.
• Embassies of many countries are located here.
• The ambassadors of other countries stay in New Delhi.
• Delhi is the largest commercial centre in Northern India.
• Climate: It is very hot in summers and very cold in winters, in Delhi.
• Places of tourist attraction:
i) Religious places - Lotus Temple, Jama Masjid, Gurdwara Sis Ganj.
ii) Monuments - Quila, India Gate, Red Fort, Qutub Minar, Humayun's Tomb, Raj Ghat.

2) Kolkata:
• Capital of West Bengal. Also called a city of joy.
• Kolkata city is situated on the banks of the river Hooghly.
• The first city to have an underground railway system called Metro.
• Kolkata has an important seaport known as Diamond Harbour.
• It is the only city to have a network of trams.
• Places of tourist attraction: Howrah Bridge, Victoria Memorial, Fort William, Eden Garden, and Salt lake stadium, etc.
• Main festival: Durga Puja.

 

3) Mumbai:
• Capital of Maharashtra. Also called a city of dreams.
• Earlier known as Bombay.
• Mumbai was a group of seven islands. Later, these islands were joined together to make Mumbai city.
• The Governor, the Chief Minister, and all other ministers stay in Mumbai.
• Mumbai is the commercial capital of India.
• It is the centre of the film industry (Bollywood).
• Mumbai High is an offshore oil field located on the west coast of Mumbai. The crude oil, which is found under the sea bed, is being extracted and refined in a refinery.
• The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre(BARC), is situated in Chembur in Mumbai, is India's first atomic power plant.
• The major languages spoken in Mumbai are Marathi, Hindi, and Konkani.
• Climate: Mumbai has warm and humid summers, winters are not very cold here. Mumbai receives heavy rainfall from June to September.
• Places of tourist attraction: Marine drive, Elephanta caves, Gateway of India, Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, Bandra-Worli sea link.
• Main festival: Ganesh Chaturthi.

 

4) Chennai:
• Capital of Tamil Nadu. Chennai was earlier known as Madras.
• Chennai - The biggest commercial and industrial centre in South India.
• It is the fourth largest city in India.
• Climate: The climate of Chennai is hot and humid throughout the year. It receives rainfall from October to December.
• Places of tourist attraction: Gandhi mandapam, Kapileshwar and Parthsarthy temples, Marina beach(It is the second largest beach in the world), Golden beach, etc.
• Main festival: Pongal.

• A river is any large natural stream of water.
• A river flows in a channel, towards the sea, ocean, lake, or into another river.
• There are two types of rivers: 
 a. Perennial rivers: Are those rivers that show a constant water flow throughout the year except under extreme conditions of drought. 
 b. Non-perennial rivers: These are the rivers that have no water for at least part of the year. Such rivers are seasonal in nature.

• The Krishna River is 4th largest river in India. It is also called Krishnaveni. Length:1,300 km.

• The Kaveri River originates in Karnataka. The river basin includes Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala, Puducherry.

• In East Central India, the Mahanadi is a major river and is very important for the state of Odisha. 

• The Narmada, also called Rewa, flows through central India. Also known as the 'Lifeline of Madhya Pradesh.'

• The Indus river is the major south-flowing river in South Asia and is the main supplier of water resources to Punjab and Sindh plains.

• The Ganges, also known as Ganga - most sacred river to the Hindus. Trans-boundary river - flows through India and Bangladesh. Originates in the Western Himalayas. Length: 2,525 km long.

• The Yamuna, also known as Jumna - one of the largest tributary river of the Ganga. Originates in the Yamunotri glacier - merges with the Ganga river at Triveni Sangam at Prayagraj. Length:1,376 km. 

• The Brahmaputra river - also called as Tsangpo. A trans-boundary river which flows through China, India, and Bangladesh. Important river in terms of irrigation, hydroelectricity generation, and transportation.

• India is a diverse country.
• Diversity means differences among individuals.
• Different religions, people, communities, castes, cultures, languages, etc. all make this country distinct.
• Diversity is due to many factors like:
1. Different geographical regions: hilly areas, deserts, plains, coastal areas, etc.
2. Different religions: Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Jainism, Buddhism, etc.
3. Different languages: Punjabi, Marathi, Sindhi, Gujarati, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, etc.
4. Different caste systems
• All these factors influence the customs, clothing, food habits, dance forms, culture, and festivals of people.
• Clothes: During the Navrati festival, Gujrati people wear ghagra-choli and perform the Garba dance.
• Bengali people wear saris during Durga pooja.
• Food: Various types of cuisines are present like South Indians prefer idli, dosa, and sambhar, while Bengali eat fish, rice and sandesh, people from Punjab eat rajma chawal.
• Dance forms: Bharatnatyam from Tamil Nadu, Odissi from Orissa, Nati from Himachal Pradesh, Bhangra from Punjab, Rouf from Kashmir etc.all these depict the diversity in the Indian culture.
• Languages: There are 22 officially recognized languages mentioned in the Constitution of India.
• Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru gave the famous phrase 'Unity in diversity'' which means despite all our differences, we are one as a nation.
• Unity in diversity was actively displayed by Indians during freedom struggle. Also it is visible during international cricket matches.
• The diversity in our country teaches us to be more tolerant towards others, to respect others, to learn from others, etc. Thus, India stands out in the world for its diversity.

• Pollution means the presence of an impurity or harmful pollutants in the environment.

Types of pollution:

1. Air pollution-
 • Air pollution is caused by hazardous gases and particles released from automobiles and industries. Also, caused by the smoke emitting from forest fires, gases emitted from decaying plant and animal materials, CFC(Chlorofluorocarbons) gases, etc.

 • Effects of air pollution: Air pollution, if severe,   leads to tuberculosis, breathing diseases, lung cancer, etc. in humans.
 - Plants are affected by low quality air.
 -The Greenhouse gases(GHGs) in the atmosphere leads to an increase in the temperature of the earth, which contributes to Global warming.

• Control measures:-
 a. Planting more trees.
 b. Using good quality petrol and diesel. Also, using clean fuels like CNG(Compressed Natural Gas).
 c. Installing Electrostatic precipitators(filtration devices) in the chimneys of the factories.
 d. Avoid the burning of crackers.
 e. Using clean energy obtained from solar cells, windmills, etc.
 f. Vehicular laws should be made more strict.

2. Water pollution-
 • Water pollution is caused by letting of untreated sewage from industries, household waste, food processing wastes, chemical fertilizers, and pesticides from agricultural fields into rivers, lakes, seas, etc.

 • Effects of water pollution: Polluted water causes diseases like typhoid, hepatitis, cholera, chickenpox, dysentery, etc. in humans.
 -Water pollution disturbs the overall ecological balance of the water body and also harms aquatic animals.

• Control measures: Industrial waste or other domestic waste should be treated before discharging them into water bodies. 
 -Drinking water should be properly treated to make it free from germs.

3. Soil pollution-
 • Soil pollution is caused by chemical fertilizers, insecticides, pesticides that are used in agriculture.

 • Effects: Agricultural runoff from the fields goes into the rivers; thus the fertilizers, pesticides, and insecticides get mixed with the river water and disturb the ecosystem there.

 • Control measures:
 a. Minimum use of fertilizers, pesticides, insecticides should be done.
 b. The use of organic products in the farms should be encouraged.

4. Noise pollution-
 • Caused by excessive sound such as blaring loudspeakers, automobiles, industries, etc.

 • Effects: Loss of hearing, loss of concentration, and lack of sleep in humans.

 • Control measures-
a. Noise barriers should be installed.
 b. More trees should be planted.

• Waste-
 • All the things that we use end up as waste.
 • Different types of waste:
 a. Solid waste, e.g., Car tyres, old books, furniture, etc.
 b. Liquid waste, e.g., Wastewater, chemical waste from industries, etc.
 c. Gaseous waste, e.g., Dust, smoke, etc.
 • Solid waste: biodegradable waste and non-biodegradable waste.

• Biodegradable waste-
 • Waste that can be broken down and decomposed into the soil by microorganisms.
 • It includes fruits, vegetable peels, leaves, wood, etc.

• Non-biodegradable waste-
 • Waste that cannot be broken down or decomposed into the soil.
 • It includes plastic, chemicals, polythene bags, etc.

• Methods of waste disposal are:

1. Sanitary landfills: Landfilling is mostly done outside the city in an open area, where the waste collected in dumpers and trucks is disposed off and spread over the land.

2. Incineration(burning): It is the process wherein the waste is burnt at high temperatures. This produces a lot of smoke and carbon dioxide, which leads to air pollution. This is the easiest and quick way to dispose off the waste.

3. Composting: It is a natural process in which the organic material gets decomposed or transformed into a rich soil called compost. This compost, when added to the garden or household plants, benefits the plant growth.

• Waste Management:
 • Waste Management includes collection, transport, processing, and monitoring of the waste.

• The 3R's are: Reduce, Recycle, and Reuse.

• Reduce: We can reduce waste by bringing some changes in our everyday habits and lifestyle. Eg. Avoid the use of plastic bags.

• Reuse: Reuse means using materials more than once. Eg. Donating old storybooks, comics to poor children.

• Recycle: Recycle means to convert a used item to another useful item. Eg. Old newspapers, plastic waste, and glass can be recycled into useful products.

• Some of the ways to reduce waste are as follows:
 a. Do not litter anywhere and do sort your waste into biodegradable and non-biodegradable.
 b. Plant more trees and conserve energy.
 c. Avoid the use of plastic bags.
 d. Use less energy and use of cleaner fuels.

East-west extent - about 2900km.

Physical Divisions of India -

India is divided into 6 divisions - 1. The Himalayan Mountain ranges 2. The Northern Fertile Plains 3. The Great Indian Desert 4. The Southern Plateau region  5. The Coastal Plains and 6. Islands.

1. The Himalayan Mountain ranges -

• Covered by snow throughout the year.

• Extend from Jammu and Kashmir in the west to Arunachal Pradesh in the east.

• 2500km - length. Width varies from 150 to 400km.

• Mount Everest (8848m) - world's highest peak - located in the Himalayan mountain range.

• Other important peaks in the Himalayas are - Mt. K2 (8611m), Mt. Kangchenjunga (8598 m), Mt. Makalu (8462m), Mt. Dhaulagiri (8167m), Mt. Nandadevi (7817m).

The Himalayas consist of 3 parallel ranges -

a) The Himadri or the Great Himalayas -

• Northernmost range.

• Includes Mount Everest (8848m) - world's highest peak. Covered by snow throughout the year.

• Consists of glaciers which are a source of many rivers like - Ganga, Yamuna, Brahmaputra, Indus etc.

• Rivers get water due to melting of snow during summer season and rainwater during the rainy season.

b) The Himachal or the Lesser Himalayas -

• Lies to the south of the Himadri.

• Is lower in height as compared to the Great Himalayas or Himadri.

• Moderate elevation - so many hill stations are found here. E.g. Srinagar, Pahalgam, Gulmarg, Shimla, Manali, Nainital, Dalhousie, Darjeeling, etc.

• Covered with coniferous forests of pine, deodar, and chir trees.

• Terrace farming is practised on the mountain slopes.

c) The Shivaliks -

• Southernmost range of the Himalayas. Lies at the base of the Himalayas.

• Hill slopes of Shivaliks - covered with thick forests rich in wildlife.

• Animals found - tigers, crocodiles, leopards, bears, sambhar deers, etc. Bhabhar and the Terai belt - Lies between the Himalayas and the Northern Plains of India.

• Bhabhar - belt consisting of big and small rock pieces.

• Terai - belt consisting of swampy and marshy land.

2. The Northern Plains -

• Located to the south of Himalayan mountain ranges.

• Flat, level land extending from Punjab in the west to Assam in the east.

• Length of around 2400 km and breadth varying between 240 to 320 km.

• Formed by 3 major river systems- the Indus, the Ganga, and the Brahmaputra along with their tributaries.

The Northern Plains are subdivided as -

a) The Punjab Plains -

• Western part of the Northern plains formed by rivers Indus along with its tributaries, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Satluj.

• Mostly lies in Pakistan and in India in the states of Punjab and Haryana.

• The Bhakra Nangal dam built on river Satluj is one of the largest dams in India.

• Agriculture is the main occupation. Wheat is the main crop grown here.

• Other important crops grown - rice, cotton, maize, sugarcane, barley and oilseeds.

b) The Ganga Plains -

• Also called - Gangetic Plains.

• Extends between river Ghaghar to River Teesta. It covers Haryana, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, and West Bengal as well as some parts of Jharkhand.

• The major rivers flowing in this region - Ganga, Yamuna, Gandhak, Kosi, and Teesta.

• River Ganga originates from the Gangotri glacier.

• Rivers Bhagirathi - joined by rivers Alakhnanda and Mandakini. The combined flow of these tributaries forms the main river, Ganga.

• Agriculture is the main occupation.

• Main crops grown - wheat, rice, sugarcane, and jute.

• This region also called as the 'food bowl of India'.

• Important towns and cities situated on the banks of river Ganga, Yamuna and their tributaries -Haridwar, Rishikesh, Delhi, Agra, Kanpur, Allahabad (now known as Prayagraj), Varanasi, Patna, Kolkata, etc.

c) The Brahmaputra Basin -

• Lies in the state of Assam.

• River Brahmaputra originates in Tibet - called as river Tsangpo. Enters India through Arunachal Pradesh. Flows through Assam, Bangladesh and drains in the Bay of Bengal.

• One of the highest rainfall regions of the world.

• Main crops grown - rice and jute. Tea - on the hill slopes. Assam - well known for tea.

3. The Peninsular Plateau or the Southern Plateau -

• Triangular landmass lying to the south of Northern Plains.

• Extends from the south of Northern plains upto Kanyakumari. Called the Peninsular plateau or the Southern plateau. River Narmada forms a boundary which divides the Southern plateau into 2 parts.

a. Central Highlands - The part located to the north of river Narmada.

b. Deccan plateau The part located to the south of River Narmada.

Main plateaus -

a. The Malwa Plateau -

• Part of the Central Highlands - located to the north of river Narmada.

• Lies between the Aravalli range and the Vindhya range.

• Fertile black soil - suitable for cultivation of cotton.

b. The Chota Nagpur Plateau -

• Situated in the northeastern part of the Southern plateau.

• Extends in - Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, and Northern Odisha.

• Rich in mineral resources - coal, iron, manganese, and mica.

• Has large iron and steel plants - Jamshedpur and Bokaro (Jharkhand), and Rourkela (Odisha).

c. The Deccan Plateau -

• Uneven, rocky surface. Covers major parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana.

• Minerals found - iron, gold, mica, coal, etc.

• Slopes towards the east.

• Important rivers -Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri

• Not as long as the rivers of northern India and are mainly rainfed.

• Many rivers become dry during the summer season.

title.en: the constitution of india- basic features

content.en:
The Constitution is a set of rules that are accepted by all people living in a country.
The necessity of a Constitution: Maintains rules, regulations, law and order as well as regulates the powers of government and provides a secure social sphere.
Making:
• The Constituent Assembly was set up for drafting the Constitution of India.
• Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the President of the Constituent Assembly.
• Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the chairman of the drafting committee.
The Constitution of India:
• Adopted on 26th November 1949
• Enforced on 26th January 1950
Significant Features:
• It is the lengthiest Constitution in the World. 
• Framework and rule-book for the Government's Legislative, Executive and Judicial bodies.
• Secularism: Allows freedom of choice of practising the religion of one's choice.
• Republic system: where people elect the head of the country.
• Sovereign country: Which is not controlled by any other country.
• Universal Adult Franchise: gives voting rights to all adult citizens
• Inspirations from different Constitutions
• Reservation of seats to weaker sections
• Combination of rigidity and flexibility with the help of amendments

content.en:
Any sentence is constructed by joining small parts. The basic parts of any sentence is a subject, a verb, and an object. When these three come together, they form a complete sentence. 

A sentence can be broadly divided into two parts. The subject and the predicate. 

The subject is the person or thing, that is doing an action, or or the person or thing that is the focus of the sentence. 

A predicate is the part of the sentence that contains the action. The predicate is formed by joining the verb and the object. 

For example

The boy is hiding behind the table. 

Here the subject is 'the boy' and 'is hiding behind the table' is the predicate which contains the verb is hiding and the object table.

Examples:

SUBJECT PREDICATE
The laptop  is kept for charging. 
Milk  is good for health. 
Agra  is known for the Taj Mahal. 
Meera  is feeling tired and wants to sleep

Abstract nouns are names of things that are not concrete. Abstract nouns are not those nouns which we can experience with our five senses. They are an intangible concept.

For example:

Love, pride, loyalty, justice, leisure etc.

 

Abstract nouns can sometimes be formed from other parts of apeech such as verbs, adjectives and also common nouns.

 

Some examples of Abstract nouns formed from adjectives

ADJECTIVE

ABSTRACT NOUN

Healthy

Health

Free

Freedom

 

Some examples of Abstract nouns formed from verbs

VERBS

ABSTRACT NOUN

Obey

Obedience

Think

Thought

 

Some examples of Abstract nouns formed from verbs

COMMON NOUNS

ABSTRACT NOUN

Patriot

Patriotism

Vegetable

Vegetarian

content.en:
A collective noun is used to refer to an entire group of persons, animals or things; it therefore includes more than one member.

For example, a ‘family’ has parents and children.

A ‘pack’ contains many wolves.

Example-

  • People: crowd, team, choir, class, committee, family, group
  • Animals: flock, herd, swarm, litter
  • Things: bunch, collection, pack, set.

More examples of collective nouns:

A team of players.

A herd of cows

A flock of sheep

A fleet of ships

Use of verb with Collective Nouns:

A plural collective noun takes a plural verb: 

Example- Families (Plural) come (Plural verb) to this restaurant.

A singular collective noun usually takes a singular verb:

Example- Our family (singular) often comes (singular verb) to this restaurant.

content.en:
There are four types of Genders:

  1. Masculine Gender
  2. Feminine Gender
  3. Neuter Gender
  4. Common Gender

Masculine Gender: The Masculine Gender denotes the names of all male persons or animals. Example:  man, actor, uncle, hero, king, lion etc. 

Feminine Gender: The Feminine Gender denotes the names of all female persons or animals. Example: woman, aunt, daughter, actress, queen, lioness etc. 

Neuter Gender: Non-living things or things without life cannot be distinguished either as male or female; hence they are called the Neuter Gender. Example: house, knife, tree, chair, table, book, ball etc. 

Common Gender: Names that can be used for both males and females are called the Common Gender. Example: child, parent, student, friend etc.  

 

Changing Masculine Noun to Feminine Noun:

1. By adding ‘ess’ to the Masculine

Example: Lion- Lioness, Prince- Princess, Host- Hostess

2. Sometimes the form is slightly changed before 'ess' is added

Example: Master- Mistress, Actor- Actress, Tiger- Tigress, God- Goddess

3. By a different word

Example: King- Queen, Boy- Girl, Father- Mother, Sir- Madam

content.en:
Nouns may be Proper Nouns, Common or Abstract.

 

A Proper Noun is the special name of a particular person or thing. It always begins with a capital letter, even in the middle of the sentence. 

For example – 

The Taj Mahal is a beautiful monument.

I live in Chennai. 

 

A Common Noun refers to people, places or things in general. 

For example – 

My friend is a doctor.

The mobile is on the table. 

 

An Abstract Noun refers to something that we cannot see or touch, but can only feel. 

For example – 

Health is wealth.

Laughter is the best medicine.

content.en:
Nouns can be one or many.

Singular nouns are those that are one and plural nouns are those nouns that are many.

Rules for changing singular nouns to plural noun.

Some nouns only add ‘s’ to the noun to make it plural.

table - tables

shop - shops

rose - roses

trees - trees

 

Some nouns which end with ‘s’, ‘ss’, ‘sh’, ‘ch’, ‘x’, or ‘o’, add ‘es’ to the noun to make it plural. 

gas -gases

glass - glasses

brush - brushes

Fox - foxes

Batch - batches

quiz – quizzes

volcano –volcanoes

 

Nouns that end with ‘y’ removes ‘y’ and add ‘ies’ to the noun. 

body– bodies

duty – duties

country – countries

 

Nouns ending with ‘f’ or ‘fe’ removes ‘f’ or ‘fe’ and adds adds ‘ves’ to the noun. 

thief – thieves

wolf - wolves

leaf - leaves

 

Some nouns do not change. They are the same in both their singular and plural forms.

deer – deer

sheep – sheep

hair – hair

 

Some nouns have irregular forms 

foot – feet

tooth – teeth

man – men

woman – women

mouse – mice

content.en:
To avoid repeating the nouns we use pronouns. In other words, pronouns take place of nouns. 

They are divided into two parts:

  • Subject Pronoun
  • Object Pronoun

Subject Pronouns replace the subject in the sentence. 


For instance: Mohit loves to play cricket. 

                        ‘He’ loves to play cricket.  


In the first sentence, ‘Mohit’ is the subject and in the second sentence the subject is replaced by a pronoun ‘he’. The pronoun used to replace the subject in the sentence is known as ‘Subject Pronoun’.


Object Pronouns replace the object in the sentence.


For instance: Pratik helps Rohan to complete the project. 


                          Pratik helps ‘him’ to complete the project. 


In the first sentence, ‘Rohan’ is the object and in the second sentence the object is replaced by a pronoun ‘him’. The pronoun used to replace the object in the sentence is known as ‘Object Pronoun’.


The following table contains examples of Subject and Object Pronouns:


Some Example sentences: 

  • I am going to the market with her.
  • We will meet them at the gate.
  • It is a new beginning for him.

content.en:
Verbs are words that show actions that are physical actions like run, jump, work and internal actions like love, think, consider etc. Without verbs, you cannot 'do' anything, 'feel' anything or even 'be' anything.  

 

They are the center of all sentences and clauses and show what the subject is doing or feeling, even if they’re just existing (being).

 

There are two categories of verbs:

 

Dynamic (action) verbs - These describe a physical action or activity. 

e.g. eat, walk, play, jump etc.

I am eating a pie.

I walk a few kilometers everyday.

I play football on the playground.

I jumped into the pool. 

 

Stative (state-of-being) verbs - Stative verbs describe a subject’s state or feeling.

e.g. want, need, like, understand etc.

I want to eat a cake.

I need to go to the doctor.

I like walking in the park.

I understood what my teacher was saying.

Verbs may be divided into Main Verbs and Helping Verbs.

 

Main Verbs are the verbs which say something about a subject. They are action words and do not require other words to complete their action. 

 

The cat jumps on the sofa.

 

Sita runs fast.

 

Mohit and Mohan play football in the ground.

 

Helping Verbs are words used to help the main verbs in a sentence. 

 

They help the main verbs express a state or an action. They are also called Auxiliary Verbs.

 

To be, do and have verbs are the most common helping verbs.

 

Use of to be verbs (is, am, are, was, were) – 

  • Is/am/are are used in Present Tense and was/were are used in the Past Tense.
  • To talk about names, age, feeling, nationality, professions and many more.

              I am Rina.         She is 15 years of age.         He was a doctor by profession. 

  • To talk about state of being

              She is tall.          We are human beings.    

 

Use of do, does, did – 

  • Do/does are used in the Present Tense and did is used in the past tense.
  • These helping verbs are used to ask questions.

                   Do you study every day?

  • They are used to indicate negative sentences.

                   She does not want to eat vegetables.

  • They are used to add emphasis to the sentences.

                   I do finish my work in class.

 

Use of have, has, had – 

  • Have/has are used in the Present tense and had is used in the Past tense.
  • These helping verbs are used to show possession.

                 She has long hair.

  • They are used when we talk of eating and drinking

                 We have coffee every day.

  • They are used with Perfect tenses

                 He has done his work.

Articles are the words ‘a’, ‘an’ or ‘the’. They are of two types – Indefinite or Definite.

Definite Article(the) is used to point out a particular person or thing. It is used both with singular and plural nouns.

THE is used-

  • When we talk about a particular person or thing

The phone is not working.

The lady who is sitting on the sofa is my mother.

 

  • Before the names of some Proper Nouns

The Arabian Sea, The Indian Ocean, The Andamans, The Taj Mahal

 

  • Before superlative degree of adjectives

This is the best day I have had in a while.

Misha is the smartest girl of this class.

 

  • Before names of things which are unique of their kind

The moon is shining in the sky.

The sky is blue.

 

  • Before singular nouns used to indicate a whole class

The elephant is a majestic animal.

The rose is the sweetest of all flowers.

 

  • Before the names of directions

The sun rises in the east.

The hills are to the west of this building.

Articles are the words ‘a’, ‘an’ or ‘the’. They are of two types – Indefinite or Definite

Indefinite Articles (a, an) does not talk about anything specific. It is always used with singular nouns.

e.g.  A book was issued by the librarian.

I was here an hour ago.

 

  • ‘An’ is always used before words that begin with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u).

             For example –

             an aeroplane     an engineer   an ice cream    an octopus    an umbrella    an hour

 

  • ‘A’ is always used before a consonant sound.

  For example –

   a bottle     a computer      a paper      a book      a watch       a university     a European

 

NOTE – The spelling of a word DOES NOT decide the use of a/an before a word. The sound of the first letter of the word (whether vowel or consonant) decides which indefinite article should be used.

Adjectives are describing words. They describe, quantify, identify or further define the qualities of nouns or pronouns.

Adjectives are mainly of five types:

  1. Adjectives of Quality
  2. Adjectives of Quantity
  3. Demonstrative Adjectives
  4. Possessive Adjectives
  5. Interrogative Adjectives

 

1. Adjective of Quality

Adjectives of quality describe the characteristics of a noun. They tell us about a noun’s size, color, shape, taste, and more. Some examples are big, yellow, square, jealous, and sweet. They answer the question ‘What kind of?’

For example: “The pink,round box is mine.” Here, pink and round are descriptive adjectives that describe the box.

 

2. Adjective of Quantity

Adjectives of quantity describe the exact or approximate amount of a noun. Some examples include all, no, few, many, and little. THey answer the question 'How much?' Numeral adjectives give exact number amounts (e.g. three, five, seventh, twelfth). They answer the question ‘How Many?’.

For example: “There are thirty girls in our class.” Here, ‘thirty’ is a numeral adjective that describes the number of girls.

There is some milk in the glass. Here, ‘some’ is an adjective of quantity that describes the approximate quantity of milk.

 

3. Demonstrative Adjective

Demonstrative adjectives answer the question ‘which one?’ They point out particular nouns. Demonstrative adjectives are this, that, these, and those.

This is used when the noun is near and singular. That is used when the noun is far and singular. These is used when the noun is near and plural. Those is used when the noun is far and plural. 

For example: “She wore that dress.” Here, that is a demonstrative adjective that points to a particular dress.

 

4. Possessive Adjective

Possessive adjectives are a type of pronoun. They explain ownership. Possessive adjectives include my, your, his, her, its, our, and their. There is a corresponding possessive adjective for each of the personal pronouns. They answer the question 'whose?' 

For example: “I lost my book.” In this sentence, my is a demonstrative adjective that explains whose book was lost.

 

5. Interrogative Adjective

Interrogative adjectives appear in interrogative sentences i.e., questions. ‘What, which, and whose’ are interrogative adjectives. In direct questions, the adjective will appear at the beginning of the sentence next to the noun it modifies.

For example: “Which book will you buy?” In this case, which is an interrogative adjective that modifies the noun book.

An adverb is a word that modifies (describes) a verb, an adjective, another adverb or a whole sentence.

 

Example:

A verb -  he talks loudly

An adjective-  very small

Another adverb-  started too quickly

or even a whole Sentence- Fortunately, I had got some money with me.

 

Examples:

Ravi is very talkative.

Ravi doesn’t talk softly.

Ramesh talks too softly.

Luckily, there was a mike so we could hear Ramesh.

 

Adverbs often end in '-ly', like - calmly, luckily, lazily, speedily, harshly, loudly etc.

 

Types of Adverbs: 

 

Adverbs of Manner- They answer the qusetion HOW?

happily, wildly noisily...

Example: The birds chirped happily in the spring.

 

Adverbs of Frequency- They answer the qusetion HOW OFTEN?

always, never, sometimes etc...

Example: He is never late for school.

 

Adverbs of Place- They answer the qusetion WHERE?

here, there, outside, back etc...

Example: The Khanna's lived there earlier.

 

Adverbs of Time- They answer the qusetion WHEN?

now, tomorrow, then, later etc...

Example: I will go to the market tomorrow.

 

Adverbs of Degree- They answer the qusetion HOW MUCH or TO WHAT DEGREE?

very, too, almost, fully, enough etc...

Example: She is fully prepared for the examination.

Conjunctions are words that join two or more words, phrases or clauses. 

Conjunctions are often used to join sentences together. The most common conjunctions include; and, or, but. 

 

They join sentences and ideas together so that the writing and reading flows smoothly.

 

The seven coordinating conjunctions are “And, but, for, nor, or, so, and yet” (Remember FANBOYS)

 

Eg: The teacher dictated the notes and we wrote it down.

 

A subordinating conjunction always introduces a dependent clause. A dependent clause is a group of words that cannot stand alone as a complete sentence. Eg: although, because, when, before, which, since etc…

 

Eg: They gave him another book because he had already read that one.

 

Correlative conjunctions are grouped conjunctions. They come in pairs. Eg: either…or, if…then, whether…or, not only…but also etc…

 

Eg: You can either go for a cruise or take a road trip.

 

  • Interjections are words used to express strong feeling or sudden emotion. 

They are included in a sentence usually at the start to express emotions like surprise, disgust, joy, excitement, or enthusiasm.

 

An interjection is not grammatically related to any other part of the sentence.

 

Eg: 

Eureka! I got the sum.

Yeah, a beautiful present.

Woo-hoo, what a goal!

Punctuations include full stops, capital letters, commas, semi-colon, question marks, exclamatory marks, apostrophe, and many more. 

 

It helps the readers to understand the meaning of the text clearly. It makes our written text logical and readable. 

 

Not using proper punctuation marks can change the meaning of the entire text. 

 

For example – 

 

            tina’s three favorite things are eating her family and shopping. (This means Tina loves to eat her family and shop)

 

           Tina’s three favorite things are eating, her family and shopping. (This means Tina loves to eat and shop and she loves her family) 

 

Capitalisation means to make the first letter of the word capital. It is used to show the readers the importance of specific words. 

 

For example – 

 

          My mother will buy dresses for me in Diwali.

 

          On Fridays, I visit my aunt’s house.

 

Formatting means the presentation of our paragraphs, essays or letters. 

 

We write headings, paragraphs, quotations, and many more in our writing skills. 

 

The way of our writing, the alignment that we show in our letters and the fonts that we use play a very important role in creating impactful writing.

 

A letter looks like a letter and a paragraph looks like a paragraph only because it follows proper formatting.

Prefixes and Suffixes are a group of letters that are added at the beginning or end of the words to create a new word with a different meaning.  


Prefixes add the letters to the beginning of the words.


For example: 

un-, multi-, over-, super-, cyber- 


Suffixes add the letters at the end of the words. 


For example: 

-ed, -er, -est, - ing, -ly, -ity, - ish, -able, -ion  


Words that come before or after a prefix or suffix are called “Root words”. 


Examples: 


Note: When the root word ends with ‘y’, replace it with the letter ‘i’ while adding the suffix to it.  


For example: 


‘happy’ – “happily”  (suffix used is ‘-ly’)


‘supply’ – “supplier” (suffix used is ‘-er’)

Homophones are words that have similar pronunciation.


They are spelled differently and their meaning also differs. 


For example: 


ate  / eight : I ate my food at eight. 


Explanation: “Ate” is the past tense of the verb ‘eat’. “Eight” is the time. 

 

Few more examples of Homophones:

Sample Sentences: 

  • I made this dish.
  • My maid helped me with cooking.


  • I do not know where to find my lost pen.
  • My mother said no for the ice-cream.


  • These seats are reserved for females and not males.
  • They have asked him to mail the documents.


  • There is so much peace around.  
  •  I will only have one piece of cake


  • I love to sit at the sea-shore. 
  • I might go to see him tomorrow.

Introduction

 

A paragraph is a group of sentences that describes a topic. The sentences are written in regular order with a unity of thought in them.  

 

       Main points for writing a paragraph

  • Introduction of the topic given for writing a paragraph.
  • Merits or demerits of the topic.
  • Conclusion.  

 

       Read the following paragraphs carefully:  

The Teacher you Like Most

Miss Reena is my English teacher. She is very beautiful. She is also an efficient teacher. Her way of teaching is fascinating. Her voice is sweet and clear. She explains a topic again and again until the students understand it completely. She is very kind and sympathetic to all the students. She does not scold anyone. She loves all the students. She is much disciplined and respectful towards all the seniors. She always gives good advice to all. She comes to school in a very simple dress. I respect her very much. She is an ideal teacher of my School.

A diary is a personal record of events, thoughts and feelings – usually arranged in chronological order. 

 

A diary is a private place where you can keep your thoughts, feelings and opinions on everything from work to school and everywhere in between. 

A diary can be your friend where you can write about and share your happiness and sorrow without the fear of being judged. 

 

While writing “Diary writing” as a creative writing task we usually follow these rules: 

  • Begin with addressing the diary, date and place.  
  • It is written in the first person from the writer’s point of view. (Use of I, we, my etc…)
  • The language can be more creative. (Use of similes, interjections, and variation in sentence length)
  • The tone can be formal or informal depending on the purpose and audience
  • Tenses can vary – diaries tend to be in the past tense but can use present tense to bring an event to life for the reader.

The Story Mountain is the easiest way to learn story writing:

 

Opening of the story: It is impressive to begin your story by describing the setting/ character or using sounds or a proverb. 

 

Eg: The park was empty, so silent as if all the birds and insects had deserted it. No children playing on the slides and swings. The creepers and wines wilting away. I felt suffocated under the monstrous banyan tree. (Describing setting)

 

Eg: Crunching and munching the potato chips leisurely lays there ‘the king of our house’. He’s such a couch potato that he wouldn’t leave the recliner even if the house is on fire. I don’t why God made brothers! To be precise, “lazy yet genius younger brothers”. (Describing character and sounds)

 

Setting: The place where story takes place. It could be a city, a village, a forest etc., or an imaginary like on other planet.

 

Characters: The characters are the people or animals in the story. It is better to keep less characters (2-3) and describe them well.

 

Conflict: The main character of the story faces a problem which is called a conflict. Eg: stuck in a flood, forgetting a wallet while in a new town, alone on an island, or animals trying to save themselves in a forest fire etc.,

 

Climax: It is when the problems reach to the peak and the character has to take some steps to solve them.

 

Resolution: It when the character is able to solve his problems.

 

Ending: It is the end of the story where all ends well. You may also have an ending that doesn’t end well. Such stories have a moral and teach the reader what one shouldn’t do. Make your ending attractive.

 

Eg:  Finally, the day ended and we all returned home safely vowing never to go on a trip in life without our parents. (Happy ending with a moral)

 

Eg:  All the caged elephants were killed. Somu was sent to a secluded island where he would be a slave now onwards. (unhappy ending)

Look at the following conversation between a mother and her child Anu.

Mother: Anu! Anu! Get up and get going! You are late for school!

Anu : Mom! I want to sleep.

Mother: Anu! You will miss the bus! Get up!

Anu: Oh yes! Thank you, mom! I will get ready in no time!

Mother: Good girl! 

A dialogue is a spoken conversation that includes at least two characters. 

Certain points should be kept in mind while writing dialogue.

a) Dialogues are written in the first person.

b) Dialogues should be brief and impactful.

c) A proper format needs to be followed while writing dialogue. The name of the speaker is always followed by a colon.

d) Interjections are widely used in dialogue writing to express the speaker’s emotions.

e) Proper punctuation to be followed in dialogue writing.
